citations: William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (New York: E. P. Dutton, 1939).
routes.history: The Manila galleons crossed the Pacific between Acapulco in New Spain and Manila from 1565 to 1815, usually one or two round trips a year. Westbound ships sailed the trade winds, carrying Mexican and Peruvian silver to buy Chinese silk and porcelain in Manila.
routes.story: Silver from American mines crossed the Pacific in these ships and paid Chinese merchants in Manila. Historians see this as the start of a truly global trade.

citations: William Lytle Schurz, The Manila Galleon (New York: E. P. Dutton, 1939).
routes.history: The return route, the tornaviaje, was worked out in 1565 by Andrés de Urdaneta. Galleons ran north to catch the westerlies and the Kuroshio current. They left Cavite at the end of June or early July and reached Acapulco around March or April of the following year, a crossing of at least four months.
routes.story: Urdaneta's discovery made the whole system possible. Before him, ships could sail west across the Pacific but not come back. Return galleons were packed with silk and porcelain, and scurvy often killed many of the crew on the long crossing.
